column11: Pesachim 117a: ‘The Gemara continues to discuss the book of Psalms. If a psalm begins with the terms nitzuaḥ or niggun, this indicates that its praise will be fulfilled in the future. Psalms that begin with the word maskil were delivered by means of a disseminator, a spokesman in a public address. The lecturer would speak softly, followed by a repetition of his discourse in the disseminator’s louder voice, so that everyone could hear. If a psalm begins: Of David a psalm, this teaches that the Divine Presence rested upon him first and afterward he recited the song. column13: Likewise, a person eventually comes to loathe all worldly physical pleasures in his old age, as written in Ecclesiastes (12) and at the end of Shabbat (152a), because being "under the sun" and subject to time, they have an expiration date in time. column15: All the more so now when the Holy One desires to straighten what was crooked, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:20): “For there is no righteous man upon earth that does good and sins not.” Meaning, where the soul once dwelt, it will certainly not allow it to be said of it that it resided in an unworthy inn; and therefore the soul will willingly humble itself to descend back into the body to revive it.

Granted, with regard to the warning against speaking evil, it is fine that Laban was warned not to harm Jacob. However, why shouldn’t he say anything good to Jacob? Rather, must one not conclude from this verse that even Laban’s good is bad in Jacob’s eyes? The Gemara concludes: Learn from this that it is so.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Nazir 23b) to illuminate his argument here (“only that his entire passion was for evil, and as stated in Nazir (23b): all the favor of the wicked is evil unto the righteous, and every blessing he wished to speak concealed what is essentially harmful to the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: For prayer demands impassioned desire and yearning, and that is the true inner root of this drive within the hearts of Israel: pure thirst for Torah and longing for Hashem's salvation; whereas among the prophets of the nations, their root is the raw lust of debauchery itself. And Onkelos investigated both these forces through necromantic attunement to the havla d'garmei of their source, immediately inquiring regarding "the judgment of that man" in Gehinnom so as to guard against adhering to the evil of that havla d'garmei—the safeguard being fear of retribution, in the manner of "pass it through fire and it shall be purified".
column15: Israel, however, falls and rises, as said: “Rejoice not against me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall arise”; therefore it is said: “The wicked are overthrown and are not, but the house of the righteous shall stand.” The explanation of this is found in Shabbat (63b) on Ecclesiastes 11:9: “Rejoice, O young man, in your youth... but know that for all these God will bring you into judgment”—up to here for words of Torah, from here onward for good deeds.

column13: And in a sacrifice, which surrenders man's total wholeness, the confirming witness is the accepting fire from heaven [which is a supernal flame spreading in man's heart, recognizing that all is given to Hashem, inflamed to surrender every faculty to Him], and within him that holy flame receives the supernal nourishment which is Hashem's desire; so it is in prayer, though this is not its place.
column15: “And God said, Let us make man.” The supreme purpose of creating the cosmos was for the creation of man, in whom the power and greatness of the Blessed Name are made manifest; for in man body and soul were joined together, which in truth are two diametric opposites, and how could they possibly unite were it not that the hand of Hashem accomplished this, He who is Singular and Unified, reconciling all polar opposites.

column11: Taanit 8a: ‘Rabbi Ami said: A person’s prayer is heard only if he places his soul in his palm, i.e., one must submit his entire soul with sincerity in his outstretched hands as he prays, as it is stated: “Let us lift up our heart with our hands” (Lamentations 3:41). column13: Certainly, nothing can stand before repentance once a person actually returns; rather, these things obstruct him from coming to repentance in the first place. column15: So too exist within the human soul two modes of prayer: namely, there is the prayer that must be continually renewed according to the changing circumstances of time, which resembles ephemeral grasses; yet from the multiplicity of prayers that a person prays intensely, an enduring spiritual potency of prayer becomes rooted within him, such that his heart prays perpetually even below conscious awareness, resembling a firmly planted, enduring tree.

column15: Herein lies the difference between Israel and the nations: Israel emanates from the Root of Will itself, empowered to bind all attributes to the divine Will; being bound not to any single attribute, but to His pure Essence, and consequently His will, blessed be He, is bound up with their will, so that all their deeds and actions proceed in accordance with the depth of the supernal Will, which is devoid of every measure; and they extend in no measure except as the depth of His will, blessed be He, illuminates for them the extent and the limit to which they may extend.

column13: However, our Sages stated: "A person should always engage in Torah not for its own sake, etc.," and that is because this condition is "always"—meaning in continuous daily routine; whereas pure study for its own sake cannot possibly be continuous, since lishmah denotes absolute meditative cleaving (devekut), whose frequency is like the conjugal time of Torah scholars once a week, for one cannot reach such devekut except on Shabbat, or for spiritual wanderers meaning those strolling in the mystical Orchard once a day at most.
column15: For the nature of the covenant sealed with the sons of Noah pertained only to the physical affairs of this world—that this temporal world should never again be destroyed—but not to eternal life in the World to Come; and the reason was that Noah contented himself with what was promised to him personally—that he himself would be among the inheritors of the World to Come—and did not exert himself to pray for his descendants after him, that an enduring remnant for eternal life should survive from him throughout future generations.

column11: Berakhot 18b: ‘In contrast to the righteous, who are referred to as living even after their death, the verse states explicitly: “The dead know nothing.” These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead, as the prophet Ezekiel said in reference to a king of Israel who was alive: “And you are a slain, wicked prince of Israel” (Ezekiel 21:30). And if you wish, say instead that the proof is from here: “At the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses the dead shall be put to death” (Deuteronomy 17:6). This is puzzling. As long as the accused has not been sentenced to death, he is alive. Rather, this person who is wicked is considered dead from the outset.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 18b) to illuminate his argument here (“wherefore the wicked in their lifetime are called dead (Berakhot 18b), for though possessing speech and biological life, since their thoughts pursue selfish lust against God's will, their essential self and heart...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And therefore the Sages taught (Berakhot 18b): the wicked in their lifetimes are called dead, for genuine life issues from the soul; but if one cleaves to corporeal lusts of the body, his soul-faculties remain mere shadows, and he is termed dead, just as upon the departure of his soul he is physically dead. But one who cleaves to Hashem God of Truth—which our Sages expounded (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1; Bereishit Rabbah 81:2; Vayikra Rabbah 26:1): why is He called Truth? Because He is the living God and eternal King.
